analysis.one_liner: Requires larger employers to give workers one to two weeks of paid vacation each year.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote; only 4 of 253 House Democrats signed on, and it died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal wage-and-hour law, to guarantee paid vacation for the first time. Employers with 100 or more workers would have to give each qualifying employee one week of paid vacation right away; after three years, employers with 50 or more workers would have to give one week, and employers with 100 or more would have to give two. Workers would need a year on the job and 1,250 hours worked to qualify, and would have to give 30 days' notice before taking the leave. The bill also directs the Labor Department to run a public awareness campaign and to study how paid leave affects productivity and health.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time workers at companies with 50 or more employees who have been there at least a year, many of whom currently get no paid vacation at all. The bill's findings note that the United States is the only industrialized country with no minimum paid-leave law, and that only 14 percent of American workers took two weeks or more of vacation in 2008. The travel and hospitality industry would also benefit from more vacation spending.

how_it_helps.text: Gives every qualifying employee at a firm with 50 or more workers a guaranteed week of paid vacation, and two weeks at firms with 100 or more, paid by the employer rather than taken as unpaid time.
Adds to federal law a benefit no other industrialized country lacks: the bill's findings state 147 countries require paid vacation and the U.S. is the only industrialized nation without such a law.

Requires the leave to be taken as a continuous block of days that cannot be rolled over, and to be separate from sick leave or leave otherwise required by law, so it cannot be absorbed by existing time off.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees, who would fund a new guaranteed paid benefit for each qualifying worker. Firms with fewer than 50 employees are exempt. In practice the cost is limited because many large employers already offer paid vacation, and only one to two weeks are required.

drawbacks.text: The mandate excludes the workers most likely to lack vacation: part-time and short-tenure workers are ineligible (12 months and 1,250 hours required), and firms with fewer than 50 employees are exempt.
Employers absorb the direct cost of paid leave, a real payroll expense for lower-margin firms, and the bill was introduced during a deep recession when businesses were cutting jobs.
The leave must be used within a 12-month period with no rollover, and workers must give 30 days' notice, which can be difficult for employees with unpredictable schedules or caregiving demands.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For covered workers, a guaranteed paid week off is a clear, concrete gain in a country with no federal vacation floor. But the bill is a modest version of the idea: one or two weeks, limited to larger firms and longer-tenure full-time workers, with use-it-or-lose-it rules and a 30-day notice requirement. The cost to employers is real but limited, and the bill's own findings argue vacation reduces stress-related health costs and absenteeism. The bigger weakness is coverage: many of the workers with the least time off would not qualify.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the Paid Vacation Act of 2009 on May 21, 2009, joined by Reps. John Lewis of Georgia and Maurice Hinchey.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced, and on October 22, 2009 sent it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
Support was thin from the start: only four members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats, out of 253 House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers avoided a new federally mandated paid-leave requirement, while workers with no paid vacation remained without one.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Democrats (the sponsor plus 4 of 253 House Democrats), no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee controlled by the Democratic majority without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would require them to fund one to two weeks of paid vacation for every qualifying worker, a new federal mandate on top of existing payroll costs. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against workers who lack any paid vacation.

The bill's own findings cite a $740 billion annual travel industry and argue more vacation means more travel spending. More guaranteed time off would direct consumer spending toward hotels, airlines, and tourism.
They are exempt from the mandate, though their workers would also remain without guaranteed vacation, putting them at a disadvantage in competing for workers against larger firms.
